HEADLINE: Tyro has small businesses in its sights
INTRO: Jost Stollmann sees a problem and an opportunity. The banks, he says, are not serving the small business community well enough. Unless a small business is able or willing to put up a house as collateral, for example, it can be very difficult to get a loan no matter how reliable the cash flow.
TEXT:
Jost Stollmann sees a problem and an opportunity. The banks, he says, are not serving the small business community well enough. Unless a small business is able or willing to put up a house as collateral, for example, it can be very difficult to get a loan no matter how reliable the cash flow.

Stollmann believes that is crippling the crucial ability of small business to grow - and damaging the Australian economy as a result. He is convinced Tyro Payments and its new banking licence can help fill that gap. Now he has a banking licence and $100 million worth of capital behind him, that dream can become a real possibility. One requirement for approval as a bank is the need for a minimum of $50 million in Tier 1 equity.

It is the first time, he says proudly, that a technology company has been granted an Australian banking licence. The general idea is to use a combination of banking skills, new technology and Stollmann's serial entrepreneurialism to offer small business customers better rates, better service and what he calls "frictionless" banking.

"Our big advantage is that we don't have all the legacy products and systems and we are entirely cloud-based," he says. "We are starting green." He concedes success will mean being dramatically better than what is already on offer, insisting he respects the power of the banks.

Nor are the banks likely to passively accept Tyro's view of the market, especially if they see another business bank - no matter how small - claiming any impact on small business lending. Think of this struggle as one more part of the coming fintech revolution. Recent research from Macquarie Bank acknowledges the banks are overly conservative when it comes to small and medium-sized business lending, requiring mortgage security in most instances. It warns banks will need to change to protect or grow profits.

"Often SMEs are left out of the equation because they are too risky/not asset-rich enough," its analysis notes.

That unmet demand, along with improving technical ability to quickly assess credit applications using large amounts of data at relatively low cost, has led to the rapid growth on online lending in the SME market in countries such as the United States. This is Tyro's opportunity too.

It is certainly a strong show of confidence that names such as Tiger Global Management from New York, TDM Asset management from Sydney and Atlassian co-founder and chief executive Mike Cannon-Brookes are backing Stollmann's ambitions here with hard cash.

But for all the pride in a $100 million capital raising and comparisons with Uber and the taxi industry, Tyro's ability to disrupt the Australian banking system is still a very early work in progress.

Banking is far more complicated than encouraging people to drive paying passengers in their cars.

Stollmann says Tyro will be able to take deposits next year but is cautious about when Australia's newest bank will actually start lending. "Watch this space," he insists."We will take it one step at a time incorporating the learnings from each step."

The amount of lending will also depend on the deposits Tyro can attract. No matter how many hundreds of software engineers Tyro employs, building a sophisticated risk management system isn't simple. Just as building a massive deposit base takes time even in this era of fast-growth fintech. But Stollmann also has a history of disruption and innovation well before these concepts became widely recognised by most in business or politics.

Twenty years ago, he was a highly successful German IT entrepreneur who walked away from an economic ministry in a new German government in 1998. Political dealmaking meant he would not play the central role he had hoped for in a restructuring of the economy. He and his family ended up in Australia several years later as part of a round-the-world sailing adventure.

Stollmann soon decided to shake up Australian banking by bringing clunky eftpos payments into the modern era with better technology. Tyro Payments was named to reflect a challenger's attempt to take on established players. The Reserve Bank, also dismayed by the lack of innovation and competition in payments, gave Tyro a special licence allowing it to take payments.

Tyro quickly developed a useful niche and now serves more than 14,000 small businesses and processes $8 billion worth of transactions annually. This includes 50 per cent of Medicare claims made through the debit card network. But that's relative to more than 550,000 merchants with eftpos terminals.

Stollmann's frustration came from the difficulty of persuading more small businesses to unbundle banking relationships. As well as the traditional reluctance to switch, he argues banks were often able to lock Tyro out of the market by offering more working capital to businesses or alternatively, implying no access to debt if businesses switched. Tyro - unable to take deposits or lend money itself - could not compete.

Now it hopes to do just that. Daily improvements in technology also make it more feasible for the growing number of fintech start-ups to challenge the dominance of the banks. That's also why the banks pronounce themselves so keen to embrace the culture of fintech themselves.

Stollmann prefers to stand apart, having opened a Tyro hub for fintech start-ups in his Sydney CBD building but insisting it remain independent of the big players. In his view, only a small window of opportunity exists - a few years at most - for Australia to develop its own fintech successes. He is delighted by the change of political tone under Malcolm Turnbull and expects next week's innovation statement to deliver the substance.

Tyro is keen to play its part. Watch this space.

HEADLINE: Atlassian fires up $5b IPO
INTRO: A gloomy market for technology floats will hang over software maker Atlassian's pursuit of a blockbuster $US3.6 billion ($5 billion) company valuation this week, but strong appetite for new shares from existing investors and its profitable track record should support the planned float.
TEXT:
A gloomy market for technology floats will hang over software maker Atlassian's pursuit of a blockbuster $US3.6 billion ($5 billion) company valuation this week, but strong appetite for new shares from existing investors and its profitable track record should support the planned float.

Former University of NSW classmates turned Atlassian founders Mike Cannon-Brookes and Scott Farquhar, alongside their Wall Street advisers, are expected to front investors after the technology firm filed a US prospectus on Friday revealing it is aiming to sell $US350 million worth of new shares.

Atlassian will become one of Australia's largest new tech listings and the co-CEOs will control a combined stake of about $US2.4 billion, if investors snap up the 20 million new shares at the estimated IPO price of between $US16.50 and $US18.50 each.

Mr Cannon-Brookes and Mr Farquhar are already the wealthiest Australians under 40 and a successful IPO would catapult them into the top 20 of the BRW Rich List.

Companies p13

HEADLINE: Paris climate deal may not be binding
INTRO: Paris | A dispute over whether a global agreement on climate change will be a legally binding treaty and subject to review later has emerged as one of the main splits over talks in Paris, where leaders from more than 140 countries will meet on Monday to initiate two weeks of negotiations.
TEXT:
Paris | A dispute over whether a global agreement on climate change will be a legally binding treaty and subject to review later has emerged as one of the main splits over talks in Paris, where leaders from more than 140 countries will meet on Monday to initiate two weeks of negotiations.

French Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius, who is chairing the United Nations COP21 conference, appeared over the weekend to give ground to US demands for a so-called hybrid agreement in which some of the carbon reduction goals outlined would be legally binding and others would not.

Such a concession from the French may be more acceptable to India and other emerging economies, which want richer nations to do more to tackle the climate change problem. But other European countries say such a proposal is not strict enough.

"The accord needs to be legally binding. It's not just literature," Mr Fabius told the Financial Times. "But it will probably have a dual nature. Some of the clauses will be legally binding."

The conference is being held under a state of emergency, with thousands of police and soldiers on the streets of Paris, coming just weeks after the November 13 terrorist attacks on the French capital.

Leaders including US President Barack Obama and Chinese President Xi Jinping will address the conference at the start of this week, after which officials will attempt to thrash out an agreement over two weeks of negotiations.

Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull has expressed support for five-year reviews of national carbon reduction targets that would require countries to track and report how they are pursuing their targets.

Such an audit mechanism has been another area of dispute among the 183 nations that have submitted emission control plans in the lead-up to this week's UN conference.

Mr Turnbull signalled he will put innovation in environmentally-friendly technologies at the heart of his pitch to world leaders on Monday, describing Labor's plan to substantially increase Australia's carbon emission reduction targets as "a heroic offer" that would be prohibitively expensive.

Speaking on the eve of the UN climate talks, Mr Turnbull indicated that any credible attempt to curb global warming would require a unified commitment from national governments to cut greenhouse emissions but also the mobilisation of the private sector to develop green technologies.

Mr Turnbull, who was speaking at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Malta on Saturday, said he hoped COP21 would result in a "a strong durable agreement" that "puts all countries on a common platform and allows them to periodically update their targets that sets us on the right path". However, the Coalition leader also linked the arguments Australia will be making in Paris over the two-week conference to his innovation agenda.

"I am optimistic that innovation and technology can play a very big part in the discussions in Paris," he said.

"The solutions to the climate change challenge lie very much in the field of technology and innovations, which is a very key part of my government's priorities. It is absolutely critical we continue to unleash that innovative spirit as we find better technologies - you just have to look at the way so many renewable technologies have improved rapidly in recent years."

He will spend Monday at COP21 with other world leaders before flying back to Australia. The leaders hope to set a positive tone for the rest of the conference whose main goal is to cap global temperature rises at 2 degrees centigrade above pre-industrial levels - a level many scientists argue will prevent climate change from having dire consequences.

Last week, Opposition Leader Bill Shorten made climate change a key battle ground for the next election by promising steeper emission cuts of 45 per cent reduction over the next 15 years, notwithstanding forecasts of significant economic and population growth over that time. He plans to go to Paris too.

UN analysis of more than 160 national carbon reduction pledges covering more than 90 per cent of global emissions will not be enough to meet the goal of capping global warming at 2C above pre-industrial levels but should instead keep temperature rises to 2.7C-3C.

HEADLINE: Big ambitions for our newest bank
INTRO: Tyro Payments started business selling payment terminals to businesses. Now, the upstart believes it can take on the banking oligopoly in one of Australia's most challenging financial markets: small business lending.
TEXT:
Tyro Payments started business selling payment terminals to businesses. Now, the upstart believes it can take on the banking oligopoly in one of Australia's most challenging financial markets: small business lending.

Backed by $100 million from prominent investors including Atlassian's Mike Cannon-Brookes and Tiger Global, Tyro was granted a full banking licence in August after a decade processing payments.

Tyro chief executive Jost Stollman said the company decided that it could use its data from 14,000 business customers to take on the established banks in lending. Macquarie Research recently estimated there is about $60 billion of unmet demand for loans from small business.

"Our goal is to build the Tyro Bank that is cloud based, totally integrated and totally mobile and that provides awesome frictionless banking solutions. Tyro spent 12 years to establish itself as a tech player, and payment provider. Now we're changing the game and we're going to a very different level," he said.

The company says its has 14,000 small and medium-sized business operating 550,000 of its payment terminals.

"But that doesn't do justice to this window of opportunity, which is we can create in Australia the next-generation bank," Mr Stollman said. "We're the only tech company that has been given a bank licence."

Tyro will not yet be able to call itself a bank but it can start taking deposits, which it can then lend. It needs a minimum of $50 million in equity to put in the application to name itself a bank and half of the $100 million is for that purpose. Some of the money will be used to hire software engineers.

Mr Cannon-Brookes, who has been on the board six years, is providing about 10 per cent of the $100 million. Last year he said the size of Australian banks' profits was an example of "insanity".

He said on top of the significance of a fintech with a bank licence, the size of the money raised itself is a big deal.

"It is huge for Australia, it is only the fourth [private raising] north of $100 million and it is the first tech deal in Australia for Tiger," he said while boarding a flight from Detroit to California to head Atlassian's $US3.6 billion ($5 billion) IPO roadshow.

He acknowledged that many other fintech small-business lenders had set up shop in Australia this year offering working capital loans but he said Tyro would be able to truly challenge the banks. "It is a bank, the cost of capital is completely different.

"We have fully government guaranteed deposits, we already have a huge acquiring business and we will be a full service bank. There's not just cash flow, there's lots of other sorts of loans we can offer.

Mr Stollman said it is too early to say what size loans the company will make, what size loan book it is targeting or what market share it wants. New small-business lenders typically loan up to $250,000 on an unsecured basis at interest rates of between 15 and 40 per cent.

They lend to businesses that generally banks would not touch because the capital cost and risk is too high to make it profitable. Therefore, they have said they are not competing with banks.

Tyro processes about 5 per cent of all card payments - the rest are done by the big four banks.

New York-based Tiger Global is a major tech investor. It counts Facebook and LinkedIn among its early-stage investments. TDM Asset Management is a $250 million fund focused on wealthy families.

A host of fintechs targeting loans to small business have cropped up in the past 18 months, including Prospa, Moula, OnDeck, Spotcap, Thincats, PayPal Credit and Kikka. But all of them are intent on working with the major banks because the banks have all the customers, distribution as well as the funding.

The most recent example is Prospa, which is in the throes of forming a referral, and possibly funding, partnership with Westpac via an online pilot where Westpac customers are referred to Prospa.

Mr Stollman said this was not true disruption: "The disrupter competes head on with the bank. The fintech who does front end innovation is just sustaining the major bank."

It is unclear if Tyro has the automated risk assessment technology that is the claimed advantage of the new fintechs but Mr Stollman said it had launched a core banking system a few weeks ago and will triple the number of software developers it employs to about 150.

HEADLINE: Westpac under fire over pay
SUBHEAD: Exclusive - Proxy firm claims bank gamed bonus measure
INTRO: Westpac Banking Corp executives, including former chief executive Gail Kelly, received millions extra in bonuses because they didn't count software costs when assessing bonuses, a proxy-advice firm claims.
TEXT:
Westpac Banking Corp executives, including former chief executive Gail Kelly, received millions extra in bonuses because they didn't count software costs when assessing bonuses, a proxy-advice firm claims.

Influential investor adviser Ownership Matters said Westpac's executives would have missed out on their long-term bonuses if cash earnings in 2013-14 were just $97 million lower and if they had been $190 million lower last financial year.

The decision to exclude a $354 million software write-off from 'cash earnings' boosted the executive's bonuses even though it hit the bank's statutory profit. Westpac's long-term bonuses are paid based on increases in the bank's cash earnings per share.

"If this write-off, under a new policy for capitalising software, had not been excluded then the cash earnings-per-share hurdle applying to half the long-term incentives due to vest at the end of 2015 would not have been met," Ownership Matters said in a report to investors.

"This means that this IT expenditure has not impacted the cash earnings as it was first capitalised and then, when written off, it was excluded from cash earnings."

Westpac denied the accounting treatment of the software had any effect of bonus payments. "There is no benefit to executives' remuneration outcomes as a result of the capitalised software write-down," a spokesman said.

Ownership Matters, which sent the report to investors last Thursday, recommended investors vote against the bank's remuneration report at its annual meeting next week.

Mrs Kelly, who retired this year, was the latest individual beneficiary of Westpac's success at beating its adjusted profit targets. She left the bank with about $11 million. Deputy chief executive Phil Coffey also benefited.

Companies have latitude to decide how to account for different kinds of expenditure. Cash spent on assets like computer systems that will contribute to profits can be treated as an asset instead of a cost and expensed over years.

Westpac's decision to exclude the software write-off from cash earnings annoyed some institutional investors because it was perceived to be designed to protect its cash earnings used to assess management performance.

The write-off was flagged as Westpac raised $3.5 billion in cash to bolster its balance sheet under pressure from the banking regulator. Westpac posted full-year cash profits of $7.8 billion.

Deutsche Bank chief executive John Cryan last week criticised bankers' pay.

HEADLINE: Councils join fossil fuel divestment campaign
INTRO: At least a dozen councils are considering selling their investments in coal, oil and gas shares and 13 councils with $5 billion invested have decided to divest from fossil fuels this year, according to activist group 350.org.
TEXT:
At least a dozen councils are considering selling their investments in coal, oil and gas shares and 13 councils with $5 billion invested have decided to divest from fossil fuels this year, according to activist group 350.org.

Most councils in Australia cannot invest in shares but have exposure to fossil fuels through term deposits with the big four Australian banks, which lend to resource companies.

At the end of last year two councils had committed to divest. That grew to total 15 this year.

Minerals Council of Australia chief executive Brendan Pearson said the 350.org report was "like all the others before it - it actually confirms that the overwhelming majority of investors are rejecting the divestment movement".

"The overwhelming majority [98 per cent] of Australia's 565 local councils are not divesting," he said.

And some of the councils that had divested, their commitments were "very guarded and partial", he said.

The Australian Capital Territory, which is both the territory and local government for Canberra, accounts for the lion's share, or $4.5 billion of the money under management for the 15 divested councils, the report said.

About 59 per cent of that, not including the ACT, is invested in with banks and financial institutions that fund fossil fuels.

Councils are constrained by credit rating requirements for their investments, so only part of that will be shifted under the string of divestment motions this year.

ACT aside, the home of the world's largest coal port, Newcastle City Council, was the most high-profile council to sell this year, as well as Melbourne. On Friday the Ballina Shire Council - in coal seam gas territory - became the country's 15th council to divest. It has $69.3 million invested.

The Sydney suburb of Randwick will assess how to change its investment policy to "allow for a comprehensive divestment from institutions supporting fossil fuels". Waverley and Woollahra, also in Sydney's eastern suburbs, have been in discussions over divestment, while community groups are lobbying Victoria's Geelong and Surf Coast Shire councils.

In Ballarat, an assessment is being run of the council's direct and indirect exposure to fossil fuel investments. Also in Victoria, a divestment strategy could be tabled at City of Yarra by Christmas.

In Western Australia, a divestment motion could be tabled at City of Perth and nearby Stirling council when both reconvene next year, while a divestment motion has been put to Bassendean council. There is also push on in the City of Adelaide.

About 495 institutions globally have committed to divest, most notably the Rockefeller Brothers Fund, one of the world's largest insurance companies Allianz, and the Norwegian Sovereign Wealth Fund. Those almost 500 institutions have $US2.6 trillion invested between them, but the amount of that subject to divestment would be a fraction.

Mr Pearson said investors would continue to reject the divestment movement because independent forecasters project that Australian coal exports will grow by 37 per cent by 2040.

"Those exports will help constrain global emissions because Australian coal is the highest quality coal in the world," he said.

Key points

Coal, oil and gas investments are under the spotlight.

But Minerals Council CEO says most investors reject divestment.

HEADLINE: Political battle hots up at home, at talks
INTRO: The political battle ground in Australia over climate change, as international talks begin in Paris, has transformed markedly into one of sharp policy differences, yet often very ill-defined aims.
TEXT:
The political battle ground in Australia over climate change, as international talks begin in Paris, has transformed markedly into one of sharp policy differences, yet often very ill-defined aims.

Having briefly become an issue that neither side really wanted to take a hard line on since the 2013 election, climate has re-emerged as a defining difference between the two sides of politics, despite or perhaps because of the elevation of Malcolm Turnbull to the prime ministership. Labor's Bill Shorten was out of the blocks early this year, announcing Labor would stick to its policy of introducing an emissions trading scheme: a move that knowingly left Labor open to a scare campaign on a new carbon tax.

In the past few days, he has gone a step further, announcing that Labor would be seeking to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 45 per cent by 2030 compared with 2005 levels, though not saying exactly how this would occur. The government has set a target of a 26 to 28 per cent cut for the same period.

Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull took aim at Mr Shorten over the weekend, describing the targets as "heroic". Mr Shorten, en route to Paris, shot back that "when it comes to climate change, Mr Turnbull is both economically irresponsible and unheroic".

Labor believes Turnbull's credibility on climate change is vulnerable because he has gone to Paris with a policy inherited from Tony Abbott, which he has previously described as "an environmental fig leaf to cover a a determination to do nothing".

The Opposition is also clearly seeking to position itself aggressively on the issue at a time when it faces as big a threat from the Greens as it does from the Coalition. With a collapsing base in the polls, it is not hard to see Shorten's announcement on greenhouse gas emissions as anything other than a little desperate.

But the Opposition Leader argues his numbers are based on the recommendations of the Climate Change Authority and therefore reflect what needs to be done if we are to properly address the issue.

The government argues that such a target would impose a cost on the economy that was too onerous and raised the spectre of Labor introducing an even larger carbon tax than the one that caused it so much grief when it was last in office.

As always, it is much more complicated than either side immediately spells out. Yes, the cost to the economy of a 45 per cent target reduction would be significant, if all other things remain equal, and if Labor was only proposing a domestic emissions trading scheme.

But as we have already seen in the past couple of years, the climate change debate - and climate change economics - is rapidly moving at an international level, and the forces determining the cost of such a policy are also constantly changing as a result.

Market forces - as financial institutions and investors increasingly worry about stranded assets - are changing the equation on returns from different energy investments. Technology is rapidly changing the cost of different energy options.

Assertions about the cost of a Labor ETS would have to be judged against the very different backdrop of the approach to renewable energy that has occurred in the past five years.

Labor has not said it would have a domestic-only ETS, something which would dramatically affect the carbon price such a system imposes. The irony here is that it has long been speculated that the Coalition might eventually morph its own Direct Action policy into one that could engage in international carbon trading.

HEADLINE: Baird hangs ten for dementia
INTRO: We all know Mike Baird can run an asset sale - but it turns out he is not a bad surfer, either.
TEXT:
We all know Mike Baird can run an asset sale - but it turns out he is not a bad surfer, either.

Fresh from signing a $10.258 billion deal for poles and wires company TransGrid, the NSW Premier spearheaded the strength-for-surfing campaign Wipeout Dementia on Saturday, which raised $80,000 for Sydney-based charity Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing (CHeBA).

Baird joined business leaders, including REA Group chairman Hamish McLennan, Andy Kennard of Kennards Storage, and Morgans banker Mark Gross, backing CHeBA's research into Alzheimer's disease and other dementias.

"We need help to get resources directed to researching prevention, diagnosis and treatment, and corporate Australia is the best hope we have for getting the volume of funds we need quickly so we can start seeing results," Genworth Mortgage Insurance chairman and CHeBA ambassador Richard Grellman told The Australian Financial Review.

Mr Grellman has first-hand experience of the high levels of care and support needed for people with dementia. His wife Suellen was diagnosed four years ago with advanced young-onset Alzheimer's disease and has been in a care facility for almost a year.

"Wipeout Dementia was an unusual concept but it worked really well in raising awareness and much-needed funds," Mr McLennan said.

HEADLINE: Hostplus plans $400m venture capital input
INTRO: Hostplus plans to invest $400 million into venture capital over the next five years, accelerating a surge of superannuation money into the sector.
TEXT:
Hostplus plans to invest $400 million into venture capital over the next five years, accelerating a surge of superannuation money into the sector.

The hospitality and sports super fund, which is responsible for just under $20 billion of members' money, has invested in Blackbird Ventures' $200 million information technology fund and Brandon Capital Partners' third Medical Research Commercialisation Fund (MRCF3) this year.

However, chief investment officer Sam Sicilia said the fund's appetite for a class of investment that super funds had historically given a wide berth was unquenched. "We have got $400 million to deploy over the next five years, just in venture capital," Mr Sicilia said.

The $52 billion First State Super plans to more than double its $120 million investment in MRCF3 to about $250 million in the short term, and the Group of Eight top research universities and the CSIRO are talking to super funds about plans to set up their own commercialisation funds.

The surging appetite of super funds for VC comes as Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull prepares to release a sweeping innovation statement on December 7 with a host of measures aimed at channelling more capital into start-ups and nurturing their growth into fully fledged businesses.

A few super funds have overcome their reluctance to embrace the high-risk, high-return challenge of investing in companies trying to turn research ideas into businesses, and the current generation of university students are keener on launching start-ups than their parents.

With the Hostplus funds growing at about 20 per cent a year - roughly doubling in size every few years - he expected to plough another $300 million into venture capital funds in the next "one to two years" and $150 million in the following years.

Mr Sicilia said about $150 million in VC funds was "about right for us at the moment" but the rapid growth of the fund meant it could continue to invest more in the sector each year and the long-term nature of their membership gave them scope to make long-term, relatively illiquid investments.

"We'd love to do more. We have got the cash, we have got the will and the desire [and] we have got the time frame," he said.

One limitation is that the fees charged by venture capital managers are higher than those of typical investment managers because of the intensive nature of the assessment process.

Industry super funds are locked in a battle with retail super funds over fees.

Mr Sicilia said the fund feared retail rivals would use the high fees charged by VC funds in their marketing.

He said Hostplus would not let that consideration deny its members the higher long-term returns of VC but it had to make sure VC did not assume too large a share of the fund to keep fees under control.

Overcoming fear of failure

The Turnbull Government's innovation statement

WHAT'S IN

■ More generous capital tax breaks for angel

investors, and more scope for start-ups to

exploit tax losses

■ More flexible US-style “Chapter 11”

bankruptcy laws to allow firms to trade out

of financial difficulties

■ Changes to R&D tax incentives to

encourage industry-research collaboration

IN BUT UNDER A CLOUD

■ New crowdfunding rules to allow

start-ups to raise capital over the internet

ON THE TABLE - not ruled in nor out

■ “Patent Box" tax breaks for profits derived

from intellectual property

■ Access to government "big data" for

research purposes

HEADLINE: Backlash derails PM's innovation policy
INTRO: A key plank of Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull's innovation statement could be undermined after industry heavyweights warned that plans to regulate crowdsourcing will suffocate start-ups.
TEXT:
A key plank of Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull's innovation statement could be undermined after industry heavyweights warned that plans to regulate crowdsourcing will suffocate start-ups.

Labor's spokesman on digital innovation, Ed Husic - who had committed bi-partisan support for crowdsourcing equity laws to be introduced into Parliament next week as part of the government's innovation policy - is threatening to withdraw Labor's support.

Innovation Minister Christopher Pyne had promised to fix crowdfunding for start-ups as its "highest priority", but the industry claims the draft legislation will make crowdfunding completely unworkable.

"The Australian government has a consistent history of surveying the world, and instead of adopting best practices or even middle of the fairway, decides to instead implement something worse that everyone else; it's employee share schemes all over again," Freelancer chief executive Matt Barrie warned, as the start-up industry's love affair with the Turnbull government faces its first major rift.

Last week Minister for Small Business and Assistant Treasurer, Kelly O'Dwyer dropped a bombshell by revealing start-ups would only be able to raise money from the general public if they are a public company with $5 million or less in assets and turnover, and that crowdsourcing limits would be capped at $5 million a year. Industry sources suggest the draft legislation may also limit retail investment to $20,000.

Ms O'Dwyer confirmed on Sunday the government would not back down from its position and would push ahead with legislation next week.

Amid the backlash, Ms O'Dwyer has assured the industry that public companies do not have to be listed and will be exempted from the usual legal requirements imposed on public companies in the Corporations Act.

"The government's legislation will provide a holiday from many of the regulatory costs," she said on Sunday in a statement. "Other countries like New Zealand do not distinguish between public and private companies, however, in Australia this is an underlying rationale of our Corporations Act and change would be complex and lengthy, delaying the introduction of [the framework] with ramifications for all businesses and investors."

Mr Husic has written to Ms O'Dwyer calling for an urgent briefing, warning Labor's bi-partisan agreement to quickly pass the laws may be off.

"We had productive talks with former small business minister Bruce Billson; in the 10 or so weeks of the Turnbull government we're yet to have a single discussion about this issue," Mr Husic told The Australian Financial Review. "We're happy to work with the government on equity crowdfunding reform but we're not going to wave through badly framed laws that might hinder - instead of aid - the growth of early stage innovation."

Founder and chief executive of MoneyPlace, Stuart Stoyan, said restrictions on crowdfunding could stunt the industry and put us further behind the rest of the word.

"Any Australian can invest in speculative mining stocks, or even gamble their life savings away at the casino. To place a cap on crowd equity investments reeks of overprotection," Mr Stoyan said.

Founder of Australia's largest equity crowdfunding platform VentureCrowd - which has raised a combined $10 million since its launch in 2013, but none for public companies - Jeremy Colless said the government was simply adopting Labour's much-criticised CAMAC report.

"The government is not cutting red tape, they are putting hurdles in the way of cash-strapped start-ups," he said.
